title: Simplification — Image Wiki
text:
Simplification
  Every element you add divides the viewer's attention, so the question about anything in the frame is never whether it is nice but what it is doing. Taking things out is the hardest edit there is.

  
    Termsimplification
    Also calledsimplicity, reduction, decluttering, less is more
    Not the same asminimalism as a style, negative space, low detail
    Read8 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Why it happensSimple is not the same as emptyThe counter-case, which is realCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Everyone finds it easy to add. You can always put in another prop, another rim light, another leaf in the corner where the frame looks thin. Every one of those decisions feels like effort, and effort feels like improvement.
Taking things out feels like giving up. It is the hardest edit in composition, and it is the one that most often turns a picture that nearly works into one that does.
The reason is arithmetic rather than taste. A viewer arrives with a fixed budget of attention and spends it on whatever is in the frame. Add a second thing and the budget splits. Add ten and there is no budget left for any of them. Simplification is the practice of deciding what the attention is being spent on, by removing the things that are spending it without earning it.
Why it happens

the subjectOne thing in the frameit is the subject by defaultthe subjectThree thingsthe eye still finds the subject, but visits the othersthe subjectTwelve thingsnothing is the subject; the frame is a fieldThe subject is identical in all three panels. Only the number of other marks changed.

The subject — marked by the small arrow — is identical in all three panels: same size, same tone, same position. The only variable is how many other marks share the frame with it.
One thing is the subject by default; there is nothing to compete. With three, your eye still finds it, but it now visits the others and comes back, and the picture has become a small tour instead of a statement. With twelve, there is no subject at all. Nothing was made weaker — the disc is unchanged — and yet it has lost, because dominance is a comparison, and it now loses eleven of them.
This is why "the subject does not stand out" is so often a problem of the background rather than of the subject.


Smashing's series on hierarchy puts it in one line: dominance is relative, and one element becomes dominant only in relation to the others (SRC-031). You can raise a subject or lower everything else, and lowering everything else is usually cheaper and always safer, because raising the subject means adding contrast, size or colour that then has to compete with whatever else in the frame already has contrast, size or colour.
There is a second mechanism on top, and it is the one people underestimate. Grouping is automatic (Gestalt grouping), so every extra element does not just take a share of attention — it also offers itself as a grouping partner for everything else. Three unrelated objects in a frame create three possible pairings and a triangle. Twelve create sixty-six pairings. Most of them are accidents, and viewers read accidents as intentions.
Photography Life's advice on this is the most practical sentence in its composition guide: work out what you are trying to say, then remove anything in the frame that works against it — and do it in the field, before the shutter, because the alternative is fixing it later (SRC-021). Their own example is walking to the tip of the peninsula that was spoiling the frame, so that it was behind the camera instead of in it.
Simple is not the same as empty
This is the distinction that decides whether a reduction worked.
A picture is simple when the few things left have jobs: something is the subject, the empty regions have shape (Negative space), and the Value structure resolves into a handful of masses that still read at thumbnail size. A picture is empty when things were removed and nothing took over the space they were using.
The test is not how much is in the frame. It is whether what remains still has a structure. This matters when you are judging images, because "clean" and "under-filled" look identical in a thumbnail and only one of them is a compliment. Ask what the largest empty region is doing; if you cannot answer, nobody composed it.



Vilhelm Hammershøi, Dust Motes Dancing in the Sunbeams, 1900 (Ordrupgaard, Copenhagen). Public domain.
Count what is in this painting. A window, a door, a skirting, a floor, and a wedge of light. No person, no furniture, no object, no incident, and almost no colour.
Now count the decisions. The window is placed off centre and pushed up so the floor gets the bottom third to itself. The wedge of sunlight enters from the right at an angle that crosses both the door and the floor, tying two flat planes together — take it away and the picture becomes two rectangles side by side. The panelled door is a fraction lighter than the wall it sits in, which is the only thing separating them.
That is why it is simple rather than empty: nothing here is available to remove. Delete any one of those five elements and something stops working.


The counter-case, which is real
Simple is not better. It is one of two strategies that both work, and Cooper Hewitt's How Posters Work makes the point structurally: the exhibition's fourteen sections include simplify and, deliberately opposite it, overwhelm the eye and assault the surface — dense pattern, competing colour, a surface bent and vandalised until it grabs you (POST-001-SUP1, POST-002).
A Bruegel is not a failed simple picture. A crowded market photograph is not a failed simple photograph. When density is the subject — a city, a crowd, an economy, a festival — reducing it would be reducing the content.


Simplify: Toulouse-Lautrec, Divan Japonais, 1893
Overwhelm: Bruegel, The Fight Between Carnival and Lent, 1559


Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, Divan Japonais, 1893. Pieter Bruegel the Elder, The Fight Between Carnival and Lent, 1559 (Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna). Both public domain.
Lautrec throws almost everything away. Jane Avril is one flat black shape from hat to hem — no folds, no modelling, no detail inside the silhouette — and the only marks allowed inside it are her face and two hands. Behind her the stage, the chairs and the orchestra are a grey wash with outlines. He even crops the singer at the top left so that her head is gone above the frame edge, leaving a body and two black gloves — a second face there would compete with the one he wants you to read.
Bruegel does the opposite deliberately. There are around two hundred figures, no focal point, and roughly even weight across the whole panel; the picture works as a field you graze rather than an arrangement you read. It has a structure — the two processions meeting in the middle — but that structure is a rule for the crowd, not a hierarchy that hands you a subject.
Neither is a botched version of the other. What would be botched is Bruegel's density with Lautrec's single subject buried inside it.


Density earns its keep when it is organised. A crowd that has been given a system — a repeating unit, a couple of value masses, a route through the frame — stays legible at any count, which is why abundance and repetition tend to travel together.



Detroit Publishing Co., Mulberry St., New York, N.Y., c. 1900 (Library of Congress). Public domain.
Hundreds of people, dozens of pushcarts, awnings, fire escapes, laundry, signage. By the arithmetic at the top of this article it should be unreadable, and it is not.
What holds it is structure rather than restraint. Two tenement walls converge on a bright gap of sky at the centre, so the frame has a route through it before you have identified a single person. The crowd sorts into three value bands — dark clothing at the bottom, pale awnings across the middle, dark buildings above. And the repeated units help: once you have read one pushcart you have read forty.
This is the honest limit of "remove things". You could not simplify this photograph without destroying its subject, which is the density itself.


Common mistakes

"It looks empty, so add something." Ask what the addition would do. If the answer is "fill the corner", it will cost you more attention than it returns.
"Simplify means crop tighter." Cropping removes context and raises tension; it also often removes the space a subject needs. Moving the camera removes an object entirely, which is the stronger edit (SRC-021).
"Simplify means less detail." Detail is not the unit. Twelve competing elements wreck a frame; one richly detailed subject does not. Drawabox works this way on purpose — pack detail where the focal point is and leave the rest bare, so the density itself does the pointing (SRC-078).
"Busy is amateur." Busy without structure is amateur. Busy with a system is Bruegel, a Persian miniature, a newspaper front page.
"The subject does not pop, so make it brighter." Try the other direction first. Lowering the competition raises the subject without adding anything to the frame (SRC-031).


Deciding what to remove

Say in one short sentence what the image is about. If you cannot, no amount of removal will help.
Squint until the picture is three or four masses. Anything that vanishes was not carrying the composition — and anything that survives but is not in your sentence is a competitor.
Take the competitors one at a time and cover each with a thumb. If nothing is lost, it was spending attention it had not earned.
Look at the corners and edges last. That is where things arrive without being invited.
Before removing anything more, check that what is left still has a subject, a value structure and empty regions with shape. If not, you have made it empty rather than simple.

              Visual hierarchy
